name: Crux
introduction: is the Southern Cross, the smallest of the 88 constellations but one of the most famous. It appears on the flags of Australia, New Zealand, Brazil, Papua New Guinea and Samoa. It is visible south of about 25° north latitude and is a constant presence in southern skies.

sections.title: What makes it special
paragraphs: The south celestial pole has no bright star, so the Southern Cross takes Polaris’s role. Extend the long axis of the cross, from [Gacrux](hip:61084) through [Acrux](hip:60718), about four and a half times its length. A line drawn perpendicularly through the middle of the Pointers, Alpha and Beta Centauri, meets it near the pole.

Ancient Greek astronomers saw these stars low on their horizon and counted them as part of Centaurus. Earth’s wobbling axis has since carried them out of sight from the Mediterranean, and European navigators recognized the cross as a separate figure in the 16th century.

image.caption: Star View schematic · catalogue positions, north up and east left
image.alt: Extending the long bar of the Southern Cross, and the perpendicular through the Pointers, leads to the south celestial pole.

sections.title: Notable stars
paragraphs: [Acrux](hip:60718), the foot of the cross, is the brightest star and a system of hot blue stars about 320 light-years away. [Mimosa](hip:62434) is a blue giant that pulsates gently every few hours.

[Gacrux](hip:61084), at the top, stands out with its orange-red color. At about 89 light-years, it is the nearest red giant of its type to the Sun and much closer than the other stars of the cross. [Imai](hip:59747) completes the figure.

sections.title: Beyond the stars
paragraphs: Beside the cross lies the Coalsack, a dark cloud of dust about 600 light-years away that blocks the light of the Milky Way. In Aboriginal Australian astronomy, it forms the head of the Emu in the Sky, a figure traced by dark lanes rather than stars. Near Mimosa, the Jewel Box cluster, NGC 4755, sparkles with blue and red stars in binoculars.
